claim: RAD21mAC cells were cultured in control EtOH conditions or in the presence of auxin (IAA) to induce rapid RAD21 degradation.
source: RAD21mAC cells were cultured in control EtOH conditions (EtOH) or in the presence of auxin (IAA) to induce rapid RAD21 degradation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a, b).
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental conditions used to degrade RAD21 protein in the cell line.

claim: Acute IAA treatment dramatically reduced mClover levels compared to control cells with a mean fluorescence intensity reduction of 82%.
source: As reported Natsume et al., 2016, acute IAA treatment dramatically reduced mClover levels compared to control cells (mean fluorescence intensity (MFI) reduction of 82%, p=2.9E-239).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative fluorescence intensity measurements with statistical significance.

claim: CTCF signal was reduced by 16% upon IAA treatment.
source: We observed a small but significant reduction in CTCF signal upon IAA treatment (mean reduction of 16%, p=1.6E-27).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements with statistical significance.

claim: SA1 levels were reduced by 22% upon IAA treatment compared to EtOH control.
source: This was similar to the mean SA1 signal which was reduced by 22% compared to EtOH control (p=3.5E-21).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements with statistical significance.

claim: SA2 levels were reduced by 63% upon IAA treatment.
source: However, SA2 levels mirrored more closely the effect on mClover, being reduced by 63% (p=1.9E-186), but not completely lost (Figure 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements with statistical significance.

claim: The retention of SA proteins despite the degradation of RAD21 was surprising given that they are considered to be part of a stable biochemical complex.
source: The retention of SA proteins despite the degradation of RAD21 was surprising given the fact that they are considered to be part of a stable biochemical complex.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data in the context of existing knowledge about cohesin complex stability.

claim: Both SA1 and SA2 interacted with RAD21 and CTCF in control cells.
source: Both SA1 and SA2 interacted with RAD21 and CTCF in control cells as expected (Parelho et al., 2008; Wendt et al., 2008), with notable differences in their preferred interactions whereby SA2 more strongly enriched RAD21 while the SA1-CTCF interaction was significantly stronger than SA2-CTCF (Figure 1c), in line with previous results (Wutz et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data and is consistent with published literature.

claim: SA2 more strongly enriched RAD21 while the SA1-CTCF interaction was significantly stronger than SA2-CTCF.
source: Both SA1 and SA2 interacted with RAD21 and CTCF in control cells as expected (Parelho et al., 2008; Wendt et al., 2008), with notable differences in their preferred interactions whereby SA2 more strongly enriched RAD21 while the SA1-CTCF interaction was significantly stronger than SA2-CTCF (Figure 1c), in line with previous results (Wutz et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data comparing SA1 and SA2 interactions.

claim: Upon RAD21 degradation, chromatin-bound SA2 levels were more strongly affected compared to SA1.
source: Upon RAD21 degradation, we again observed a stronger effect on chromatin-bound SA2 levels compared to SA1, suggesting that SA2 is more sensitive to cohesin loss than SA1.
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data comparing SA1 and SA2 after RAD21 degradation.

claim: Residual SA proteins retained their ability to interact with CTCF in the absence of RAD21.
source: Residual SA proteins retained their ability to interact with CTCF in the absence of RAD21 and additionally, the interaction between SA1 and CTCF was further enhanced (Figure 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data showing SA-CTCF interactions after RAD21 degradation.

claim: The interaction between SA1 and CTCF was further enhanced upon RAD21 degradation.
source: Residual SA proteins retained their ability to interact with CTCF in the absence of RAD21 and additionally, the interaction between SA1 and CTCF was further enhanced (Figure 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data showing enhanced SA1-CTCF interaction after RAD21 degradation.

claim: Reciprocal coIPs with CTCF confirmed the CTCF-SA interactions in RAD21-depleted cells, including the differences between SA1 and SA2.
source: Reciprocal coIPs with CTCF confirmed the CTCF-SA interactions in RAD21-depleted cells, including the differences between SA1 and SA2 (Figure 1d).
evidence: The claim is supported by reciprocal co-immunoprecipitation experiments.

claim: Approximately 20% of SA1 and SA2 were bound to chromatin without RAD21 even in unperturbed RAD21mAC HCT116 cells.
source: We also confirmed that approximately 20% of SA1 and SA2 were bound to chromatin without RAD21 even in unperturbed RAD21mAC HCT116 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d), reminiscent of reports of that SA1 can be independent of cohesin at telomeres (Bisht et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by GFP-TRAP data and is consistent with published observations at telomeres.

claim: In control RAD21mAC cells, CTCF, SA1 and SA2 localizations exhibited clustering as quantified by cluster analysis and nearest neighbor distance analysis.
source: In control RAD21mAC cells, we observed clustering of CTCF, SA1 and SA2 localizations as quantified by cluster analysis and nearest neighbor distance (NND) analysis of protein clusters (Ricci et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by STORM imaging data analyzed using established methods.

claim: SA1 and CTCF exhibited higher densities compared to SA2, with shorter distances between clusters.
source: SA1 and CTCF exhibited higher densities compared to SA2, with shorter distances between clusters (mean NND of 68.9, 65.3, and 78.9 nm for CTCF, SA1 and SA2, respectively) (Figure 1f and g).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative STORM imaging data.

claim: Both SA1 and SA2 exhibited significant co-localization with CTCF at short distances in RAD21mAC cells.
source: Furthermore, we analyzed the relative distribution of SA clusters to CTCF clusters by assessing the NND distribution between SA1 and CTCF, and SA2 and CTCF. Both SA1 and SA2 exhibited significant co-localization with CTCF at short distances in RAD21mAC cells (Figure 1h and Figure 1—figure supplement 1f, g).
evidence: The claim is supported by nearest neighbor distance analysis from STORM imaging.

claim: Upon IAA treatment, a decreased density of detected SA1, SA2, and CTCF was observed in two analyzed clones.
source: Upon IAA treatment, we observed a decreased density of detected SA1, SA2, and CTCF in two analyzed clones (Figure 1e and f and Figure 1—figure supplement 1e), suggesting that RAD21 degradation affects the stability of SA proteins and CTCF.
evidence: The claim is supported by STORM imaging data from two independent clones.

claim: SA2 localizations were more affected than SA1 upon RAD21 degradation.
source: As observed by conventional confocal microscopy (Figure 1b), SA2 localizations were more affected than SA1 (mean density reduction in SA1, 32% and SA2, 42% compared to EtOH controls).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative STORM imaging data comparing SA1 and SA2.

claim: SA1, SA2, and CTCF clusters were more sparsely distributed across the nucleus upon RAD21 degradation.
source: Accordingly, SA1, SA2, and CTCF clusters were more sparsely distributed across the nucleus upon RAD21 degradation (mean NND 81.1, 109.7 and 117.5 nm, respectively) with SA2 significantly more affected than SA1 (mean NND increase 24.3%, 39% respectively) (Figure 1g).
evidence: The claim is supported by nearest neighbor distance analysis from STORM imaging.

claim: SA proteins and CTCF remained co-localized upon RAD21 degradation as compared to both the control cells and to a simulation of randomly-distributed protein clusters at the same density.
source: SA proteins and CTCF remained co-localized upon RAD21 degradation as compared to both the control cells and to a simulation of randomly-distributed protein clusters at the same density (Figure 1h and Figure 1—figure supplement 1f, g).
evidence: The claim is supported by nearest neighbor distance analysis comparing experimental data to simulated random distributions.

claim: The probability of SA1 at CTCF is only modestly affected upon RAD21 degradation, while SA2 at CTCF is more affected.
source: Interestingly, while the probability of SA1 at CTCF is only modestly affected, SA2 at CTCF is more affected in IAA-treated cells (Figure 1h), in line with our previous observations.
evidence: The claim is supported by nearest neighbor distance analysis comparing SA1 and SA2 localization to CTCF.

claim: Both global and CTCF-overlapping RAD21 and SMC3 ChIP-seq signals were dramatically lost in IAA-treated cells.
source: In contrast, both global and CTCF-overlapping RAD21 and SMC3 ChIP-seq signals were dramatically lost in IAA-treated cells (Figure 1i and Figure 1—figure supplement 1h).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data comparing control and IAA-treated cells.

claim: Residual SA1 and SA2 binding sites were detected in IAA-treated cells which retained a substantial overlap with CTCF.
source: In agreement with our microscopy and biochemistry results, we detected residual SA1 and SA2 binding sites in IAA-treated cells which retained a substantial overlap with CTCF.
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data showing SA binding sites overlapping with CTCF after RAD21 degradation.

claim: The sites co-occupied by CTCF and SA proteins in RAD21-depleted cells were also bound in control conditions, were enriched at TSSs and were characterized by active chromatin marks including phospho-S5 POLR2A, H3K4me3, and H3K27ac.
source: Furthermore, the sites co-occupied by CTCF and SA proteins in RAD21-depleted cells were also bound in control conditions, were enriched at TSSs and were characterized by active chromatin marks including phospho-S5 POLR2A, H3K4me3, and H3K27ac (Figure 1i and Figure 1—figure supplement 1i).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data and ChromHMM analysis showing enrichment of active chromatin marks.

claim: CTCF and SA maintain occupancy at their canonical binding sites in the absence of RAD21, suggesting that SA interaction with CTCF in the absence of the cohesin ring is a step in normal cohesin activity.
source: Thus, CTCF and SA maintain occupancy at their canonical binding sites in the absence of RAD21, suggesting that SA interaction with CTCF in the absence of the cohesin ring is a step in normal cohesin activity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the ChIP-seq data suggesting a functional role for SA-CTCF interactions independent of cohesin.

claim: Depletion of cohesin results in a dramatic loss of Topologically Associated Domain (TAD) structure.
source: While depletion of cohesin results in a dramatic loss of Topologically Associated Domain (TAD) structure (Rao et al., 2017), the frequency of long-range inter-TAD, intra-compartment contacts (LRC) is increased (Sofueva et al., 2013; Rao et al., 2017), and enriched for CTCF (Sofueva et al., 2013) or active elements (Rao et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by published Hi-C data from cohesin-depleted cells.

claim: The frequency of long-range inter-TAD, intra-compartment contacts (LRC) is increased upon cohesin depletion.
source: While depletion of cohesin results in a dramatic loss of Topologically Associated Domain (TAD) structure (Rao et al., 2017), the frequency of long-range inter-TAD, intra-compartment contacts (LRC) is increased (Sofueva et al., 2013; Rao et al., 2017), and enriched for CTCF (Sofueva et al., 2013) or active elements (Rao et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by published Hi-C data from cohesin-depleted cells.

claim: Long-range contacts are enriched for CTCF or active elements upon cohesin depletion.
source: While depletion of cohesin results in a dramatic loss of Topologically Associated Domain (TAD) structure (Rao et al., 2017), the frequency of long-range inter-TAD, intra-compartment contacts (LRC) is increased (Sofueva et al., 2013; Rao et al., 2017), and enriched for CTCF (Sofueva et al., 2013) or active elements (Rao et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by published Hi-C data from cohesin-depleted cells.

claim: Local TAD contacts are lost and clustered LRCs are enriched in IAA conditions.
source: As previously shown (Rao et al., 2017), local TAD contacts are lost and clustered LRCs are enriched in IAA conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by re-analysis of published Hi-C data from IAA-treated RAD21mAC cells.

claim: SA-CTCFΔcoh are enriched at the clustered LRCs formed when cells are depleted of cohesin.
source: We probed the Hi-C datasets for contacts containing the residual SA-CTCFΔcoh binding sites and observed a further enrichment in IAA conditions (Figure 1j, bottom right), indicating that SA-CTCFΔcoh are enriched at the clustered LRCs formed when cells are depleted of cohesin and thus implicating them in 3D structural configurations.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of Hi-C data overlapped with ChIP-seq data for SA-CTCF binding sites.

claim: Cohesin-independent SA, either with CTCF or alone, may itself contribute to higher order arrangement of active chromatin and regulatory features in 3D space.
source: Our results suggest that cohesin-independent SA, either with CTCF or alone, may itself contribute to higher order arrangement of active chromatin and regulatory features in 3D space.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Hi-C and ChIP-seq data suggesting a functional role for SA in 3D genome organization.

claim: SA proteins contain a highly conserved domain known as the 'stromalin conservative domain' (SCD) or the 'conserved essential surface' (CES).
source: SA proteins contain a highly conserved domain known as the 'stromalin conservative domain' (SCD) (Orgil et al., 2015; Roig et al., 2014), or the 'conserved essential surface' (CES).
evidence: The claim is supported by published structural and functional studies of SA proteins.

claim: A F/YXF motif in the N-terminus of CTCF engages with a composite binding surface containing amino acids from RAD21 and the CES of SA2, forming a tripartite interaction patch.
source: Structural analysis of CTCF-SA2-RAD21 has shown that a F/YXF motif in the N-terminus of CTCF engages with a composite binding surface containing amino acids from RAD21 and the CES of SA2, forming a tripartite interaction patch (Li et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by published structural analysis of the CTCF-SA2-RAD21 complex.

claim: A similar F/YXF motif was identified in other cohesin regulatory proteins, predicting interactions between the SA-RAD21 binding surface and additional chromatin proteins.
source: Further, the authors identified a similar F/YXF motif in other cohesin regulatory proteins, predicting interactions between the SA-RAD21 binding surface and additional chromatin proteins.
evidence: The claim is based on published predictions of protein-protein interactions based on motif analysis.

claim: All the F/YXF-motif containing proteins (CTCF, CHD6, MCM3, HNRNPUL2) interacted with SA1 in RAD21-control cells and their interaction with SA1 was enriched upon RAD21-degradation.
source: All the proteins interacted with SA1 in RAD21-control cells and their interaction with SA1 was enriched upon RAD21-degradation, indicating that the association was not dependent on the amino acids contributed by RAD21.
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data showing SA1 interactions with F/YXF-motif proteins.

claim: The association between SA1 and F/YXF-motif proteins was not dependent on the amino acids contributed by RAD21.
source: All the proteins interacted with SA1 in RAD21-control cells and their interaction with SA1 was enriched upon RAD21-degradation, indicating that the association was not dependent on the amino acids contributed by RAD21.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the co-immunoprecipitation data showing maintained interactions after RAD21 degradation.

claim: Despite SA2 also containing the conserved CES domain, the F/YXF-motif proteins showed little interaction with SA2.
source: Interestingly, despite SA2 also containing the conserved CES domain, the F/YXF-motif proteins showed little interaction with SA2 (Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 1b), pointing to the presence of additional features in SA1 that stabilize its interaction with F/YXF containing proteins in vivo.
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data comparing SA1 and SA2 interactions with F/YXF-motif proteins.

claim: Additional features in SA1 stabilize its interaction with F/YXF containing proteins in vivo.
source: Interestingly, despite SA2 also containing the conserved CES domain, the F/YXF-motif proteins showed little interaction with SA2 (Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 1b), pointing to the presence of additional features in SA1 that stabilize its interaction with F/YXF containing proteins in vivo.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential interactions observed between SA1 and SA2 with F/YXF-motif proteins.

claim: SA proteins, independent of the cohesin trimer, bind to DNA and RNA.
source: We show that SA proteins, independent of the cohesin trimer, bind to DNA and RNA, either in the context of RNA:DNA hybrid structures, as we have shown here, or perhaps sequentially, and facilitate the loading of cohesin.
evidence: The claim is supported by CLIP and ChIP-seq data showing SA binding to nucleic acids in the absence of cohesin.

claim: SA1 IP-MS identified 136 high-confidence interactors whose abundance was significantly altered with RAD21 loss.
source: We used a pairwise analysis of IAA vs UT SA1 samples to generate a fold-change value for each putative interactor. These candidates were changed by at least 1.5-fold compared to UT controls, and sensitive to siSA1, yielding 136 high-confidence interactors whose abundance was significantly altered with RAD21 loss (SA1ΔCoh; Figure 2b and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data with defined statistical criteria.

claim: Core cohesin subunits SMC1A and SMC3 were strongly depleted in SA1 IP-MS from IAA-treated cells while no peptides were detected for RAD21.
source: As expected, core cohesin subunits SMC1A and SMC3 were strongly depleted while no peptides were detected for RAD21.
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data showing loss of cohesin subunits.

claim: The vast majority of the SA1ΔCoh interactors were enriched for binding with SA1 in IAA conditions (117 of 136).
source: In line with the enrichment we observed for the CES-binding proteins in IAA-conditions (Figures 1c and 2a), the vast majority of the SA1ΔCoh interactors were enriched for binding with SA1 in IAA conditions (117 of 136), and represent cohesin-independent SA1ΔCoh interactors (Figure 2b).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of mass spectrometry data.

claim: RNA processing was the most enriched category in the SA1ΔCoh PPI network (FDR = 3.62 × 10–39).
source: RNA processing was the most enriched category in the SA1ΔCoh PPI network (FDR = 3.62 × 10–39) and included proteins involved in RNA modification (YTHDC1, ADAR1, FTSJ3), mRNA stabilization and export (SYNCRIP, FMR1), and RNA splicing regulators (SRSF1, SON) (Figure 2c).
evidence: The claim is supported by STRING analysis of the SA1ΔCoh interactome with statistical significance.

claim: There was a significant enrichment for DNA and RNA helicases (FDR = 3.54 × 10–08) in the SA1ΔCoh PPI network.
source: We also found a significant enrichment for DNA and RNA helicases (FDR = 3.54 × 10–08) as well as RNA binding proteins (FDR = 9.11 × 10–11) within which were many HNRNP family members (HNRNPU, aka SAF-A).
evidence: The claim is supported by STRING analysis of the SA1ΔCoh interactome with statistical significance.

claim: There was a significant enrichment for RNA binding proteins (FDR = 9.11 × 10–11) in the SA1ΔCoh PPI network.
source: We also found a significant enrichment for DNA and RNA helicases (FDR = 3.54 × 10–08) as well as RNA binding proteins (FDR = 9.11 × 10–11) within which were many HNRNP family members (HNRNPU, aka SAF-A).
evidence: The claim is supported by STRING analysis of the SA1ΔCoh interactome with statistical significance.

claim: There was a highly significant enrichment of proteins associated with ribosome biogenesis (FDR = 2.20 × 10–30) in the SA1ΔCoh PPI network.
source: We also found a highly significant enrichment of proteins associated with ribosome biogenesis (FDR = 2.20 × 10–30) including both large and small subunit components; rRNA processing factors and components of the snoRNA pathway (FDR = 4.39 × 10–05).
evidence: The claim is supported by STRING analysis of the SA1ΔCoh interactome with statistical significance.

claim: Translation was significantly enriched as a biological process (p=1.64 × 10–06) in the SA1ΔCoh PPI network.
source: Finally, translation was significantly enriched as a biological process (p=1.64 × 10–06), with several cytoplasmic translation regulators identified as SA1ΔCoh interactors (DHX29, GCN1L1).
evidence: The claim is supported by STRING analysis of the SA1ΔCoh interactome with statistical significance.

claim: Both SA1 and SA2 directly bound RNA as evidenced by CLIP.
source: We performed SA-crosslinking and immunoprecipitation (CLIP) in untreated RAD21mAC cells and found that both SA1 and SA2 directly bound RNA (Figure 3a and b).
evidence: The claim is supported by CLIP experiments showing RNA binding to SA proteins.

claim: Cohesin is not required for the interaction of SA1 and SA2 with RNA in cells.
source: As before, RAD21 depletion reduced SA1 and SA2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1d) and the amount of RNA crosslinked remained proportional to the amount of residual SA1 and SA2 protein (Figure 3c and Figure 3—figure supplement 1e), demonstrating that cohesin is not required for the interaction of these proteins with RNA in cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by CLIP experiments in RAD21-depleted cells showing maintained RNA binding.

claim: Nuclear S9.6 levels were significantly reduced in cells overexpressing ppyCAG-RNaseH-V5 (38% of controls, p=0.04).
source: IF using the R-loop specific antibody S9.6 revealed that nuclear S9.6 levels were significantly reduced in cells which expressed V5 (38% of controls, p=0.04) and that mean SA1 signal was significantly reduced by 29% in the same cells (Figure 3d).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data showing reduced R-loops upon RNaseH overexpression.

claim: Mean SA1 signal was significantly reduced by 29% in cells overexpressing RNaseH.
source: IF using the R-loop specific antibody S9.6 revealed that nuclear S9.6 levels were significantly reduced in cells which expressed V5 (38% of controls, p=0.04) and that mean SA1 signal was significantly reduced by 29% in the same cells (Figure 3d).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data showing reduced SA1 upon RNaseH overexpression.

claim: S9.6 IF signal was significantly increased in siAQR and siSA1 but not siSA2 cells compared to the siScr control.
source: Furthermore, RAD21mAC cells treated with scramble control siRNAs or Smartpool (SP) siRNAs to AQR (a known suppressor of R-loops Sollier et al., 2014), SA1 or SA2 revealed that S9.6 IF signal was significantly increased in siAQR and siSA1 but not siSA2 cells compared to the siScr control (mean S9.6 signal increased by 28%, p=0.0004; 32%, p=3.90E-8; reduced by 10%, p=0.17, respectively; Figure 3—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data showing increased R-loops upon SA1 knockdown.

claim: Upon IAA treatment, SA1 localizations were significantly enriched within S9.6 domains (mean ratio 1.24, p<0.0001).
source: However, upon IAA treatment, we observed a significant enrichment of SA1 localizations within S9.6 domains (mean ratio 1.24, p<0.0001; Figure 3e), strongly suggesting that SA1 proteins are localized within R-loop domains independently of cohesin.
evidence: The claim is supported by STORM imaging data showing SA1 enrichment in R-loop domains after RAD21 degradation.

claim: Both the custom R-loop interactome as well as proteins from individual studies were highly over-enriched in the SA1ΔCoh interactome (FDR = 1.1 × 10–15, 1.4x10–47, 7.7x10–19, respectively).
source: Both the custom R-loop interactome (termed 'overlap') as well as proteins from the individual studies were highly over-enriched in the SA1ΔCoh interactome (FDR = 1.1 × 10–15, 1.4x10–47, 7.7x10–19, respectively; Figure 3f).
evidence: The claim is supported by hypergeometric distribution analysis comparing SA1ΔCoh interactome with published R-loop interactomes.

claim: S9.6 precipitated the known R-loop helicases AQR, DHX9, RNase H2 as well as MCM3 and RNA Pol II.
source: In agreement with published results, we found that S9.6 precipitated the known R-loop helicases AQR, DHX9, RNase H2 (Sollier et al., 2014; Cristini et al., 2018) as well as MCM3 and RNA Pol II (POLR2) (Skourti-Stathaki et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by S9.6 co-immunoprecipitation data and is consistent with published results.

claim: Both SA1 and SA2 precipitated with S9.6.
source: Both SA1 and SA2 precipitated with S9.6 and treatment with RNase H (RNH) revealed the specificity of the S9.6-SA interactions since the reduction of R-loop signal was proportional to the observed reduction in coIP of SA1 by S9.6 (Figure 3g and Figure 3—figure supplement 1h, i).
evidence: The claim is supported by S9.6 co-immunoprecipitation data showing SA protein interactions with R-loops.

claim: 50,338 RNH-sensitive R-loop sites were detected which were also sensitive to acute degradation of RAD21.
source: We detected 50,338 RNH-sensitive R-loop sites which were also sensitive to acute degradation of RAD21, albeit not to the same extent as RNH treatment (average S9.6 signal was reduced by 31.4% in RNH and 16.8% in IAA compared to EtOH control; Figure 3h and i).
evidence: The claim is supported by DRIP-seq data comparing RNaseH and IAA treatments.

claim: A small proportion of R-loop sites directly overlapped with SA1/2, RAD21 and CTCF in control EtOH conditions.
source: Among the RNH-sensitive R-loop sites, we detected two regimes of SA-R-loop biology. A small proportion of R-loop sites directly overlapped with SA1/2, RAD21 and CTCF in control EtOH conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of DRIP-seq and ChIP-seq data showing overlapping binding sites.

claim: R-loop sites that overlapped with SA1/2, RAD21 and CTCF were enriched at genes and both the SA1 and SA2 read density was sensitive to RAD21 loss.
source: These sites were enriched at genes and both the SA1 and SA2 read density was sensitive to RAD21 loss (Figure 3h and i and Figure 3—figure supplement 1j, k).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of DRIP-seq and ChIP-seq data showing changes upon RAD21 degradation.

claim: A larger proportion of R-loops had SA signals adjacent (bound within 2 kb of the R-loop peak).
source: On the other hand, a larger proportion of R-loops had SA signals adjacent (bound within 2 kb of the R-loop peak).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of DRIP-seq and ChIP-seq data showing SA binding near R-loops.

claim: SA sites adjacent to R-loops were enriched in repressed chromatin and were not sensitive to RAD21 loss, in fact their read density was enriched compared to EtOH controls.
source: Interestingly, these SA sites were enriched in repressed chromatin and were not sensitive to RAD21 loss, in fact their read density was enriched compared to EtOH controls (Figure 3h and i and Figure 3—figure supplement 1j, k), reminiscent of the enrichment observed previously by STORM imaging (Figure 3e).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of DRIP-seq and ChIP-seq data showing enrichment of SA at adjacent R-loops after RAD21 degradation.

claim: mClover signal was robustly lost in IAA conditions and was partially restored to EtOH levels within 4 hr of IAA withdrawal.
source: We assessed this by measuring mClover signal intensity using IF and observed that it was robustly lost in IAA conditions and was partially restored to EtOH levels within 4 hr of IAA withdrawal (Figure 4a and b and Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data showing RAD21 reloading after IAA washoff.

claim: In NIPBL KD conditions, mean RAD21 re-loading efficiency was reduced to 58% of siCon, although this was not statistically significant (p=0.33).
source: As expected, in NIPBL KD conditions, mean RAD21 re-loading efficiency was reduced, although surprisingly, this was incomplete (58% of siCon; mean re-loading siNIPBL, 2.1 vs siCon, 3.6), and did not represent a statistically significant difference (p=0.33) (Figure 4d and e and Figure 4—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by chromatin fractionation and immunoblot data showing partial RAD21 reloading without NIPBL.

claim: Cells can still load cohesin in the absence of NIPBL.
source: This result was reproduced using IF, where mean mClover signal in siNIPBL-treated cells was 54.9% of siCon (MFI siCon, 6563 vs siNIPBL, 3602) (Figure 4g), indicating that cells can still load cohesin in the absence of NIPBL.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data showing RAD21 reloading in NIPBL-depleted cells.

claim: SA KD had a more dramatic effect on cohesin re-loading efficiency than NIPBL KD, reducing RAD21 on chromatin to 37% of siCon.
source: In both population and single cell analysis of reloading, SA KD had a more dramatic effect on cohesin re-loading efficiency than NIPBL KD, reducing RAD21 on chromatin to 37% of siCon (mean siSA, 1.9 vs siCon, 5.1, p=0.002 for (Figure 4f and Figure 4—figure supplement 1d). MFI siCon, 6563 vs siSA, 2303 p<0.0001 for Figure 4g).
evidence: The claim is supported by chromatin fractionation, immunoblot, and immunofluorescence data comparing SA and NIPBL knockdowns.

claim: In the absence of both SA and NIPBL, cohesin reloading was reduced further.
source: In the absence of both SA and NIPBL, cohesin reloading was reduced further (mean siNIPBL +siSA, 1.4 vs siCon, 5.1, p=0.001 for (Figure 4f and Figure 4—figure supplement 1d). MFI siCon, 6563 vs siNIPBL +SA,1925 p<0.001 for Figure 4g), indicating that SA performs an important and complementary step to NIPBL during normal reloading.
evidence: The claim is supported by chromatin fractionation, immunoblot, and immunofluorescence data showing additive effects of SA and NIPBL knockdowns.

claim: Cohesin reloading was more efficient in siSA2 (where SA1 is present) than in siSA1 (where SA2 is present), and siSA1 was similar in reloading to siSA.
source: We observed that cohesin reloading was more efficient in siSA2 (where SA1 is present) than in siSA1 (where SA2 is present), and that siSA1 was similar in reloading to siSA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: The claim is supported by chromatin fractionation and immunoblot data comparing SA1 and SA2 knockdowns.

claim: The bulk of the reloading in RAD21mAC cells treated with IAA is supported by SA1.
source: Together these observations suggest that the bulk of the reloading in RAD21mAC cells treated with IAA is supported by SA1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effects of SA1 and SA2 knockdowns on cohesin reloading.

claim: mClover signal was not significantly changed upon treatment with Triptolide compared to IAA washoff conditions, indicating that RNA is not a key determinant of cohesin reloading per se.
source: While a significant reduction in nascent RNA signal was detected upon treatment with Triptolide (TRP), mClover signal was not significantly changed compared to IAA washoff conditions, indicating that RNA is not a key determinant of cohesin reloading per se (Figure 4h, left panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data measuring RAD21 and nascent RNA after transcription inhibition.

claim: A significant increase in nascent RNA was observed upon acute RAD21 degradation which returned to EtOH levels when cohesin became reloaded onto chromatin.
source: However, we did observe a significant increase in nascent RNA upon acute RAD21 degradation which returned to EtOH levels when cohesin became reloaded onto chromatin (Figure 4h, right panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data measuring nascent RNA incorporation during RAD21 degradation and reloading.

claim: The increase in nascent RNA in IAA conditions was no longer detected in cells treated with siRNA to SA1.
source: Again, we observed an increase in nascent RNA in IAA conditions compared to EtOH control, but this was no longer detected in cells treated with siRNA to SA1 (Figure 4i).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data measuring nascent RNA in SA1-depleted cells.

claim: SA1 plays a role in the stabilization of nascent RNA in the absence of cohesin.
source: Our results point to a role for SA1 in the stabilization of nascent RNA in the absence of cohesin and a possible competition between SA-RNA and SA-cohesin associations.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the nascent RNA data in the context of SA1 knockdown.

claim: In EtOH conditions, RAD21 localizations were depleted from the S9.6 domain (mean ratio 0.95).
source: Interestingly, in EtOH conditions, RAD21 localizations were depleted from the S9.6 domain (mean ratio 0.95; Figure 4j) similar to what we observed for SA1 (Figure 3h).
evidence: The claim is supported by STORM imaging data measuring RAD21 localization relative to R-loop domains.

claim: Upon IAA washoff, new RAD21-mClover molecules became significantly enriched within S9.6 domains compared to EtOH treated cells (mean ratio 1.19, p=0.029).
source: Upon IAA washoff, new RAD21-mClover molecules are readily detected, became significantly enriched within S9.6 domains compared to EtOH treated cells (mean ratio 1.19, p=0.029) and were sensitive to treatment with RNase H (mean ratio 0.98; Figure 4j).
evidence: The claim is supported by STORM imaging data showing RAD21 enrichment in R-loop domains after reloading.

claim: Reloaded RAD21 enrichment in S9.6 domains was sensitive to treatment with RNase H (mean ratio 0.98).
source: Upon IAA washoff, new RAD21-mClover molecules are readily detected, became significantly enriched within S9.6 domains compared to EtOH treated cells (mean ratio 1.19, p=0.029) and were sensitive to treatment with RNase H (mean ratio 0.98; Figure 4j).
evidence: The claim is supported by STORM imaging data showing loss of RAD21 enrichment after RNaseH treatment.

claim: SA1 proteins play a role in mediating reloading of cohesin at R-loops.
source: Overall, our results point to a role for SA1 proteins in mediating reloading of cohesin at R-loops.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the STORM imaging data showing RAD21 enrichment at R-loops after reloading.

claim: One prominent transcript variant arises from the alternative splicing of a single C-terminal exon, exon 31 in SA1 (SA1e31∆) and exon 32 in SA2 (SA2e32∆).
source: We found that one prominent variant is highly conserved in human HCT116 cells AND mouse embryonic stem and neural progenitor cells, arises from the alternative splicing of a single C-terminal exon, exon 31 in SA1 (SA1e31∆) and exon 32 in SA2 (SA2e32∆; Figure 5a, inset).
evidence: The claim is supported by VAST-tools analysis of RNA-seq data from multiple datasets.

claim: The majority of SA1 mRNAs include e31 (average 'percent spliced in' (PSI) 97.7% in HCT cells).
source: The majority of SA1 mRNAs include e31 (average 'percent spliced in' (PSI) 97.7% in HCT cells), while the majority of SA2 mRNAs exclude e32 (average PSI 20.4% in HCT; Figure 5b, Table 1 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1a, b).
evidence: The claim is supported by VAST-tools analysis of RNA-seq data showing differential exon inclusion.

claim: The majority of SA2 mRNAs exclude e32 (average PSI 20.4% in HCT).
source: The majority of SA1 mRNAs include e31 (average 'percent spliced in' (PSI) 97.7% in HCT cells), while the majority of SA2 mRNAs exclude e32 (average PSI 20.4% in HCT; Figure 5b, Table 1 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1a, b).
evidence: The claim is supported by VAST-tools analysis of RNA-seq data showing differential exon inclusion.

claim: Specific targeting of SA1 e31 led to a reduction of 85% of SA1 compared to esiRNA control.
source: Specific targeting of SA1 e31 led to a reduction of 85% of SA1 compared to esiRNA control (which was comparable to SP KD).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data showing SA1 knockdown with exon-specific esiRNA.

claim: SA2 e32 targeting had a minimal effect on SA2 protein levels compared to its esiRNA control (reduction of 2%).
source: In contrast, SA2 e32 targeting had a minimal effect on SA2 protein levels compared to its esiRNA control (reduction of 2%; Figure 5c), in line with the PSI data (Figure 5b) and indicating that the dominant SA2 isoform does not contain e32.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data showing minimal SA2 knockdown with exon-specific esiRNA.

claim: The amino acid sequence of the spliced SA exons encode a highly basic domain within an otherwise acidic C-terminus.
source: Interestingly, the amino acid (aa) sequence of the spliced SA exons encode a highly basic domain within an otherwise acidic C-terminus (Figure 5a, inset).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of the amino acid sequence and isoelectric point of the alternatively spliced exons.

claim: e31 and e32 have retained their basic properties (pI = 10.4 and 9.9, respectively) despite divergence in N- and C-termini sequences between SA paralogs.
source: Overall, the SA paralogs are highly homologous, however the N- and C-termini diverge in their aa sequence. Despite this, e31 and e32 have retained their basic properties (pI = 10.4 and 9.9, respectively).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of amino acid sequence conservation and isoelectric point calculations.

claim: The presence of e32 did not change the ability of SA2 to interact with RNA.
source: While the presence of e32 did not change the ability of SA2 to interact with RNA (Figure 5d, blue arrows), cells expressing the alternative exon routinely enriched RBPs with molecular weights ~110–140 kDa (Figure 5d, black arrow), strongly suggesting that the e32 domain may act to stabilize the association of SA2 with RBPs.
evidence: The claim is supported by CLIP data comparing SA2 isoforms with and without exon 32.

claim: Cells expressing SA2 with the alternative exon 32 routinely enriched RBPs with molecular weights ~110–140 kDa.
source: While the presence of e32 did not change the ability of SA2 to interact with RNA (Figure 5d, blue arrows), cells expressing the alternative exon routinely enriched RBPs with molecular weights ~110–140 kDa (Figure 5d, black arrow), strongly suggesting that the e32 domain may act to stabilize the association of SA2 with RBPs.
evidence: The claim is supported by CLIP data showing enrichment of specific RBPs with SA2 containing exon 32.

claim: The e32 domain may act to stabilize the association of SA2 with RBPs.
source: While the presence of e32 did not change the ability of SA2 to interact with RNA (Figure 5d, blue arrows), cells expressing the alternative exon routinely enriched RBPs with molecular weights ~110–140 kDa (Figure 5d, black arrow), strongly suggesting that the e32 domain may act to stabilize the association of SA2 with RBPs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the CLIP data showing differential RBP enrichment with SA2 isoforms.

claim: A mild enrichment for post-translational modification category was observed from the SA2e32∆ IP (FDR = 0.0234, p=1.35e-06).
source: GO analysis of proteins changed by at least 1.5-fold, and absent in Mock IP revealed a mild enrichment for post-translational modification category from the SA2e32∆ IP (FDR = 0.0234, p=1.35e-06), and conversely an enrichment of the RNA Binding category from SA2e32+ (FDR = 3.43E-05, p=6.56E-09).
evidence: The claim is supported by GO analysis of mass spectrometry data comparing SA2 isoforms.

claim: An enrichment of the RNA Binding category was observed from SA2e32+ IP (FDR = 3.43E-05, p=6.56E-09).
source: GO analysis of proteins changed by at least 1.5-fold, and absent in Mock IP revealed a mild enrichment for post-translational modification category from the SA2e32∆ IP (FDR = 0.0234, p=1.35e-06), and conversely an enrichment of the RNA Binding category from SA2e32+ (FDR = 3.43E-05, p=6.56E-09).
evidence: The claim is supported by GO analysis of mass spectrometry data comparing SA2 isoforms.

claim: The enriched proteins included YTHDC1 and YTHDF3, DIS3 and POLR2B, all known to play key roles in RNA-protein complexes and stability, have molecular weights ~110–140 kDa.
source: Interestingly, the enriched proteins included YTHDC1 and YTHDF3 (previously identified in the SA1ΔCoh interactome, Figure 2b), DIS3 and POLR2B, all known to play key roles in RNA-protein complexes and stability, have molecular weights ~110–140 kDa and thus likely represent the specifically enriched band in the CLIP experiments (Figure 5d, black arrow).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data identifying specific RBPs enriched with SA2e32+.

claim: SA2e32+ was more enriched in the S9.6 IP compared to SA2e32∆ (enrichment of 1.8-fold and 1.24-fold respectively, relative to endogenous SA2).
source: We repeated the S9.6 IP in RAD21mAC cells expressing either YFP-SA2e32+ or YFP-SA2e32∆. As before, AQR and MCM3 were enriched by S9.6 IP (Figure 5f) and we found that SA2e32+ was more enriched in the S9.6 IP compared to SA2e32∆ (enrichment of 1.8-fold and 1.24-fold respectively, relative to endogenous SA2; Figure 5f and g).
evidence: The claim is supported by S9.6 co-immunoprecipitation data comparing SA2 isoforms.

claim: The alternatively spliced C-terminal basic domain of SA stabilizes interactions with RBPs and R-loops.
source: Taken together, our results support a role for the alternatively spliced C-terminal basic domain of SA in stabilizing interactions with RBPs and R-loops.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the CLIP, mass spectrometry, and S9.6 IP data comparing SA2 isoforms.

claim: SA1 has a previously unappreciated role in post-transcriptional regulation of gene expression.
source: These observations suggest that SA1 has a previously unappreciated role in post-transcriptional regulation of gene expression which offers much-needed new insight into its roles in disease and cancer.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the SA1 interactome data showing enrichment of RNA processing factors.

claim: SA proteins are required for loading of cohesin to chromatin in cells deficient for NIPBL.
source: Importantly, SA proteins are required for loading of cohesin to chromatin in cells deficient for NIPBL.
evidence: The claim is supported by reloading experiments showing reduced cohesin loading in SA-depleted cells.

claim: SA1 takes advantage of structural R-loop platforms to link cohesin loading and chromatin structure with diverse functions.
source: We propose that SA1 takes advantage of structural R-loop platforms to link cohesin loading and chromatin structure with diverse functions.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the data showing SA1 localization at R-loops and its role in cohesin loading.

claim: Mutations of cohesin subunits lead to changes in cellular identity, both during development and in cancer.
source: Accordingly, mutations of cohesin subunits lead to changes in cellular identity, both during development and in cancer (Leiserson et al., 2015; Horsfield et al., 2007; Viny and Levine, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by published studies on cohesin mutations in development and cancer.

claim: Cohesin contributes to cell identity changes in large part by dynamically regulating 3D genome organization and mediating communication between distal regulatory elements.
source: A prevailing model is that cohesin contributes to cell identity changes in large part by dynamically regulating 3D genome organization and mediating communication between distal regulatory elements (Hadjur et al., 2009; Sofueva et al., 2013; Zuin et al., 2014; Kojic et al., 2018; Rao et al., 2017; Wutz et al., 2017; Fudenberg et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is based on a prevailing model supported by multiple published studies.

claim: The SA subunit is the subunit most commonly mutated across a wide spectrum of cancers.
source: Rarely is the SA subunit considered for its roles independent of the cohesin ring, even though it is the subunit most commonly mutated across a wide spectrum of cancers (Leiserson et al., 2015; Balbás-Martínez et al., 2013; Solomon et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by published cancer genomics studies.

claim: The yeast SA orthologue is critical for efficient association of cohesin with DNA and its ATPase activation.
source: The yeast SA orthologue is critical for efficient association of cohesin with DNA and its ATPase activation (Murayama and Uhlmann, 2014; Orgil et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by published biochemical studies in yeast.

claim: Separating interactions into SA-loader and cohesin ring-loader sub-complexes still impairs cohesin loading, indicating that SA functions as more than just a bridge protein.
source: Separating interactions into SA-loader and cohesin ring-loader sub-complexes still impairs cohesin loading, indicating that SA functions as more than just a bridge protein (Orgil et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by published biochemical studies showing SA's role beyond bridging.

claim: NIPBL and SA interact together and wrap around both the cohesin ring and DNA to position and entrap DNA.
source: Of note, NIPBL and SA interact together and wrap around both the cohesin ring and DNA to position and entrap DNA (Li et al., 2018; Shi et al., 2020; Higashi et al., 2020), implying a potential role for SA in the initial recruitment of cohesin to DNA alongside NIPBL.
evidence: The claim is supported by published structural studies of the cohesin loading complex.

claim: SA proteins bridge the interaction between cohesin and CTCF.
source: Further, SA proteins bridge the interaction between cohesin and CTCF (Li et al., 2018; Xiao et al., 2011; Saldaña-Meyer et al., 2014), and also bridge interactions with specific nucleic acid structures in vitro (Bisht et al., 2013; Lin et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by published structural and biochemical studies.

claim: SA1 binds to AT-rich telomeric sequences.
source: SA1 binds to AT-rich telomeric sequences (Bisht et al., 2013; Lin et al., 2016) and SA2 displays sequence-independent affinity for particular DNA structures commonly found at sites of repair, recombination, and replication (Countryman et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by published in vitro DNA binding studies.

claim: SA2 displays sequence-independent affinity for particular DNA structures commonly found at sites of repair, recombination, and replication.
source: SA1 binds to AT-rich telomeric sequences (Bisht et al., 2013; Lin et al., 2016) and SA2 displays sequence-independent affinity for particular DNA structures commonly found at sites of repair, recombination, and replication (Countryman et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by published in vitro DNA binding studies.

claim: Cohesin captures the second strand of DNA via a single-strand intermediate in vitro.
source: In vitro experiments show that cohesin captures the second strand of DNA via a single-strand intermediate (Murayama et al., 2018), and chromatid cohesion is impaired by de-stabilization of single-strand DNA intermediates during replication (Zheng et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by published in vitro biochemical studies.

claim: Chromatid cohesion is impaired by de-stabilization of single-strand DNA intermediates during replication.
source: In vitro experiments show that cohesin captures the second strand of DNA via a single-strand intermediate (Murayama et al., 2018), and chromatid cohesion is impaired by de-stabilization of single-strand DNA intermediates during replication (Zheng et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by published studies in yeast.

claim: During transcription, the elongating nascent RNA can hybridize to the template strand of the DNA and form an R-loop, which is an intermediate RNA:DNA hybrid conformation with a displaced single strand of DNA.
source: During transcription, the elongating nascent RNA can hybridize to the template strand of the DNA and form an R-loop, which is an intermediate RNA:DNA hybrid conformation with a displaced single strand of DNA (García-Muse and Aguilera, 2019).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about R-loop formation during transcription.

claim: Co-transcriptional RNA processing, splicing, and messenger ribonucleoprotein (mRNP) assembly counteract R-loop formation.
source: For example, co-transcriptional RNA processing, splicing, and messenger ribonucleoprotein (mRNP) assembly counteract R-loop formation (Crossley et al., 2019; Li and Manley, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by published studies on R-loop regulation.

claim: R-loop structures regulate transcription of mRNA by recruitment of transcription factors, displacement of nucleosomes, and preservation of open chromatin.
source: R-loop structures have also been shown to regulate transcription of mRNA by recruitment of transcription factors, displacement of nucleosomes, and preservation of open chromatin (Boque-Sastre et al., 2015; Powell et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by published studies on R-loop functions.
